answer: LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding, Tang et al., 2015) preserves first-order proximity by defining, for each edge (i, j), a joint probability distribution over the two endpoints, p1(vi, vj) = 1 / (1 + exp(-u_i·u_j)), where u_i are the vertex embeddings. This is matched against the empirical distribution p̂1(vi, vj) = w_ij / W (edge weight normalized by total weight) by minimizing the KL-divergence, which reduces to an objective over observed edges only, using negative sampling for efficiency. Because the objective only considers directly connected vertex pairs (and their observed weights), it never looks at paths, multi-hop neighborhoods, or the global topology of the graph; LINE's second-order variant instead uses a context-vector objective so that vertices sharing many neighbors get similar embeddings. First-order proximity alone is considered sufficient for real-world graphs because such networks are very large, sparse, and noisy, and the edges that exist are the most reliable signal of closeness: strongly connected vertices tend to be similar (homophily and the tendency of real ties to reflect relations), so local pairwise relations capture most of the useful structure. Restricting to edges keeps the optimization scalable (linear in the number of edges, enabled by edge sampling and negative sampling) and avoids the cost of computing global structure such as multi-hop random walks, while the combination of first- and second-order proximity covers more of the neighborhood structure in practice.
